title: Gov. Cox says Utah Republicans must rebuild voter trust after major midterm losses

 SALT LAKE CITY (KUTV) — Utah Gov. Spencer Cox said Monday that Republicans must take a hard look at their policies and leadership following significant Democratic gains in the 2026 midterm elections, warning that voters have sent a clear message to elected officials who have failed to listen to their concerns.
 During his monthly news conference, Cox described the election results as a rejection of the Republican Party, both nationally and in Utah.
 “The state of the Republican Party nationwide, and it’s not great,” Cox said.
 He acknowledged that he underestimated the extent of the Democratic gains in Utah, particularly in state legislative races.
 “I’ve followed Utah politics most of my life, and I can’t remember anything quite like what we saw last Tuesday,” Cox said.

 The governor pointed to concerns over housing affordability, government transparency, redistricting and data center development as issues frustrating voters.
 He also suggested Republican lawmakers had ignored public opposition to certain policies, including changes to voter-approved ballot initiatives and legislation affecting public employee unions.
 Cox said lawmakers should be particularly cautious about altering initiatives approved by voters.
 “I’ve warned the legislature about this many times over the years,” Cox said. “They change initiatives at their own peril.”
 He acknowledged that the election results could give him greater influence over legislation after Republicans lost their veto-proof supermajority.
 “It means I can stop some things from happening that maybe I couldn’t before,” Cox said.
 However, he stopped short of predicting whether he would issue more vetoes during the upcoming legislative session.
 Cox also addressed President Donald Trump’s role in the Republican losses.
 “The president certainly shares some blame for what happened in this election,” Cox said.
 Despite the criticism, Cox said he maintains a good working relationship with Trump and hopes the administration will reconsider its approach following the results.
 He said the cost of living, concerns about corruption, the war in Iran and immigration as major issues influencing voters nationally, citing exit polling.
 Looking ahead to the legislative session, Cox said his administration would continue prioritizing efforts to save the Great Salt Lake, reduce housing costs and address the effects of social media on children.
 On another issue, Cox expressed strong support for Utah Attorney General Derek Brown’s legal actions against prediction market operator Kalshi, including criminal charges against two of its founders.
 “They can go do their thing somewhere else, but they’re not gonna do it here,” Cox said, arguing that the company is violating Utah’s constitutional prohibition on gambling.
 Despite the challenges facing Republicans, Cox said he believes the party can regain voters’ trust by responding to their concerns and avoiding political extremes.
 “People are desperate for normal,” Cox said.
 He warned that Republican candidates heading into the 2028 elections will need to demonstrate they understand why voters rejected the party in 2026.
 “We’re gonna have to work really hard to build back the trust of Utahns,” Cox said.
